title: Retrieval Practice Enhances Learning in Real Primary School Settings
author: Laura Franzoi, Veronica Cembrani, Claudio Mulatti, and Barbara Treccani
summary: This Frontiers in Psychology study tests whether two well-established laboratory findings, the testing effect and the spacing effect, hold up with authentic curriculum material in a real primary school. Thirty-three Italian fifth graders in two classes studied history texts developed with their teachers, either by rereading or by completing fill-in-the-gap tests with answer-key feedback and self-correction until every blank was correct, and the interval between first reading and the study session was set at either one or four days. Across a four-phase quasi-experimental design, testing reliably outperformed rereading, but lengthening the spacing interval alone produced no significant benefit. The authors argue the null spacing result may reflect their minimal, schedule-friendly manipulation, the masking effect of already-strong retrieval practice, or one day already being enough, and they note a harder expository text may have obscured effects. They situate the findings within research showing students and teachers favor rereading and cramming because of misleading feelings of fluency. The paper closes by recommending fill-in-the-gap testing as a practical classroom tool and calling for teacher training, curriculum integration, and research on distributed practice, mathematics, and learners with disabilities. It was surfaced by Episcopal Academy CTL's Beacon roundup.
points: With authentic history texts and fifth graders, fill-in-the-gap retrieval with corrective feedback produced better retention than rereading, replicating the testing effect outside the lab.

Extending the gap between initial reading and study from one to four days produced no significant improvement, a result the authors attribute partly to their minimal, schedule-friendly spacing design.
Rereading creates an 'illusion of competence' through familiarity, which helps explain why students and even teachers continue to favor it and cramming over effortful strategies.
The authors recommend fill-in-the-gap tests as quick, targeted, low-cost tools that double as learning activities and allow students to self-assess with corrective feedback.
Limitations include a small convenience sample, incomplete counterbalancing across phases, and group testing conditions, so the spacing null result should be read cautiously.
quotes: In line with existing literature, our findings support the advantage of the testing procedure over the simple re-reading of the material for enhancing 5th graders' learning. In contrast, the manipulation of the spacing interval did not yield a significant effect on students' performance, suggesting the need to explore other sustainable approaches to implement distributed practice.

We found that testing promotes better learning than re-reading, in line with previous literature. However, in contrast to findings from prior studies, the spacing interval alone (i.e., in Phase 4) did not affect students' performance in our study.

This kind of manipulation aimed to minimally affect the regular lesson schedule of the two classes participating in the experiment, thus ensuring the ecological validity of the study, which was one of our main goals. Moreover, if successful, it could have provided a convenient and straightforward method for implementing this effective learning approach in primary school classrooms: two sessions, separated by a reasonable amount of time—only a few days—seem to be a feasible and acceptable way of applying distributed practice.
Our results, however, suggest that the benefits of lengthening the delay between study sessions may be more limited than previously thought and/or dependent on specific conditions.

The use of fill-in-the-gap tests provides several advantages in the educational context. Firstly, these tests offer a more interactive and engaging way for students to demonstrate their comprehension of the topic. By allowing students to recall and apply their knowledge to complete the missing parts of a sentence or passage, fill-in-the-gap tests promote active engagement and deeper processing of the material.
